where: Section 1, sentence after the two conditions
problem: "Both must be absent before we call a process reversible" contradicts the two conditions just listed. The quasi-static condition is something that must be present; only the dissipative effects must be absent. Read literally, the sentence tells a student that a reversible process must not be quasi-static.
fix: The first condition must hold and the second must be met: no finite gradients anywhere inside or across the boundary, and no dissipative effect. Then, and only then, is the process reversible.

where: Section 3, last sentence of the internal/external paragraph
problem: "when a problem says reversible without qualification, it usually means internally reversible" goes against the standard definition, where reversible without qualification means totally reversible, i.e. both internally and externally reversible. A student may write this in an exam as the definition.
fix: Standard texts define a reversible (totally reversible) process as one that is both internally and externally reversible. Many numerical problems only need internal reversibility, so check whether the surroundings are also idealised before assuming total reversibility.

problem: "...the whole 29.84 kJ that could have been exported is destroyed as ordered energy" suggests work was turned into heat. Free expansion of an ideal gas is adiabatic and the internal energy and temperature do not change, so no energy is destroyed; only the work potential is lost. The 29.84 kJ is the lost work, equal to T₀ times the entropy generated in the gas (300 × 0.5 × 0.287 × ln 2 ≈ 29.84 kJ).
fix: "Work lost = 29.84 − 0 = 29.84 kJ. For an ideal gas in free expansion the temperature does not change and no heat is absorbed, so no energy is destroyed; what is lost is the 29.84 kJ of work that the reversible path could have delivered. That lost work equals T₀ × entropy generated = 300 × 0.0995 ≈ 29.84 kJ."
